summary:
LUNARIS (Lunar Navigation, Illumination & Rescheduling Intelligence System) is an interactive lunar landing-site navigator that transforms NASA data into understandable, actionable mission-planning decisions. Visitors explore ten terrain-modeled study points near the lunar south pole across 426 days, select an arrival time and mission duration, and see where the Sun and Earth appear relative to the local terrain horizon. A 3D Moon, first-person surface views, visibility timelines, site/date comparisons, and operating-window measurements make complex lunar geometry intuitive.


Built on NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter/LOLA elevation models and JPL NAIF SPICE ephemerides, with geometric direction checks against JPL Horizons, LUNARIS goes beyond visualization. Users enter mission-specific sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility requirements, evaluate possible arrivals, simulate a landing delay, identify the constraint that is violated, and search for new opportunities without relaxing those requirements. Its explainable results, explicit treatment of uncertainty, and reproducible scientific data make lunar exploration more accessible to mission-concept teams, educators, students, and the public.
details:
THE CHALLENGE AND THE IDEA

Near the Moon’s south pole, sunlight approaches the horizon at low angles. Ridges and crater rims can obstruct the Sun and Earth from a particular location. A candidate study point therefore cannot be evaluated by its coordinates alone: arrival time, duration, terrain, and operational needs all matter. LUNARIS brings these dimensions together in one intuitive application, giving mission planners, educators, and the public a fast way to explore landing sites and dates.

AN INTERACTIVE LUNAR LANDING-SITE NAVIGATOR

In Mission, users explore a rotatable 3D Moon and ten NASA-sourced lunar south-pole study points, each supported by its own terrain-aware model. They choose a site, a UTC arrival, and a mission duration; enter a first-person surface view; inspect the Sun and Earth above the local landscape; and move through the cached timeline. The application shows their azimuth and elevation, whether terrain obstructs their centers, visibility intervals, the longest interruptions, and periods when both are simultaneously visible. A guided walkthrough introduces the experience without specialist software. LUNARIS also shows the time remaining before the next Sun or Earth visibility interruption, helping users anticipate critical operational windows.

Compare evaluates different study points and arrivals under a shared duration and set of assumptions, exposing the trade-off between solar access and direct-to-Earth opportunities. The opportunity explorer searches date/site combinations on an explicit time grid, showing when a different location or start date offers more confirmed operating time. Nine additional Apollo, NASA CLPS, and international lunar mission locations are available for geographical exploration using clearly distinguished level-horizon geometry.

DISRUPTION-AWARE, EXPLAINABLE REPLANNING

LUNARIS’s distinctive feature is the connection between environmental data and decision-making. A user can define a maximum sunlight-unavailable interval, maximum Earth-center obstruction, minimum total simultaneous visibility, and minimum uninterrupted simultaneous visibility. These limits represent a selected mission concept and can be edited to match its planning requirements. The application evaluates the full mission period and returns a constraint-based result with numerical margins, time intervals, and supporting evidence.

Its landing-delay demonstration makes the workflow concrete. A 12-hour illustrative mission initially meets its four selected requirements on 1 November 2026 at 06:00 UTC. Delaying arrival by 72 hours changes the lighting geometry: a 12-hour interval without qualified Sun visibility exceeds the selected 7-hour maximum by 5 hours. LUNARIS identifies the reason and finds the next confirmed start on the specified hourly search grid—17 November 2026 at 03:00 UTC—without changing the original requirements. The same approach can be used to compare alternative sites, dates, and mission durations.

NASA DATA AND THE COMPUTATIONAL ENGINE

The scientific engine combines NASA LRO/LOLA local 5 m/pixel elevation products, regional 80 m/pixel and outer-regional 240 m/pixel terrain with JPL NAIF SPICE solar-system ephemerides and lunar orientation kernels. For each observer, it calculates local Sun and Earth directions and evaluates them against curved lunar terrain horizons. Geometric directions have been cross-checked with JPL Horizons. The application distinguishes qualified, blocked, and unresolved intervals, and presents its model assumptions and source provenance alongside reproducible decision records. The time-domain engine covers 426 days, from 1 November 2026 through 31 December 2027.

TOOLS AND ARCHITECTURE

Python is used for scientific data processing and deterministic calculations, including SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, Pillow, and supporting geospatial libraries. The web application uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js and a responsive, GPU-accelerated 3D scene; Vite and Node.js support development and testing. The finished experience is distributed as a publicly accessible GitHub Pages site with precomputed scientific data and local browser assets, rather than requiring visitors to install specialist analysis software. The project includes numerical and browser regression tests, exact source records, dataset hashes, and a public code repository.

ORIGINALITY, IMPACT, AND INTENDED USERS

LUNARIS is not merely a lunar map or a visual ephemeris. It turns Sun/Earth geometry into explainable decisions, visualizes the consequences of a missed arrival, and recommends alternative opportunities under the same requirements. It combines rigorous terrain-aware computation with an accessible design that can be explored during a short demonstration or examined in depth through its scientific documentation. Its intended users include mission-concept researchers, student engineering teams, teachers, science communicators, and the public. The result is a reusable way to understand how lunar operations depend on both where and when a spacecraft arrives.

SCIENTIFIC INTERPRETATION

Results evaluate geometric visibility under user-selected constraints. Sun visibility indicates an opportunity for direct solar illumination; Earth-center visibility indicates a geometric direct-to-Earth path. They are useful planning inputs and are distinct from spacecraft electrical power budgets, radio-link engineering, and formal landing-safety certification.
